newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO in bid to finalise Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO in bid to finalise Hebron deal.

text.p: Israel and the PLO were to try on Monday to finalise their Hebron deal on Monday after removing the main obstacle during a lightning mediation mission to Gaza and Tel Aviv by Jordan's King Hussein.

Negotiators would meet in Jerusalem at 0800 GMT to draft final points in the deal, including a compromise reached on Sunday for the completion of three Israeli troop withdrawals from rural West Bank areas by mid-1998, officials said.
News of a possible deal angered members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government and representatives of the Jewish settlers in the occupied Arab territories.

A timeframe for the pullbacks, originally scheduled to be completed by September this year, has been the main stumbling block to sealing a deal on implementing a long overdue Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"King Hussein, U.S. envoy Dennis Ross and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu telephoned Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and told him Netanyahu has accepted the formula," said a PLO official who asked not to be identified.

"I think because of the important initiative that His Majesty took we have made considerable progress and I think we can envision the end of the negotiations in sight," Netanyahu said after meeting the monarch late on Sunday.
Officials from both sides said a summit between Netanyahu and Arafat could be held within 48 hours.

The PLO had been reluctant to sign an accord on Hebron, where some 400 Jewish settlers live amid more than 100,000 Palestinians, without a commitment from Israel to carry out the additional West Bank pullbacks agreed in previous peace deals.

Israel had proposed to complete the West Bank pullbacks by May 1999 and the United States suggested mid-1998. The PLO had demanded Israel stick to a 1995 peace deal signed by Israel's previous left-leaning government under which the withdrawals were to have been completed by September this year.
News of the compromise angered members of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition government and at least seven ministers on his 18-member cabinet were expected to oppose the deal.

"This is very severe in our eyes. I doubt the prime minister will obtain a majority (for the deal)...We hope this government will not contribute to the previous government's mistakes," said Transport Minister Yigal Bibi of the National Religious Party.
Jewish settlers called an "emergency meeting" and warned that an Israeli withdrawal would lead to bloodshed.

"The agreement is liable to create an extremely severe and dangerous situation here," said Noam Arnon, spokesman for the Hebron settlers. The West Bank town has been a flashpoint for Arab-Israeli violence.
King Hussein discussed the mid-1998 compromise during talks on Sunday in Gaza with Arafat and by telephone with Egyptian leader Hosni Mubarak. The king then flew to Tel Aviv to see Netanyahu.
"I think there was significant progress on the subjects that are not connected with Hebron," Netanyahu said in a clear reference to the three West Bank pullbacks.
A PLO official said Israel and the Palestinians had agreed to start the first of the three West Bank rural redeployments on February 28.

King Hussein told the Tel Aviv news conference: "I believe...we are on the verge of the completion of a long road and as far as I'm concerned, I leave here confident that everything will move in the right direction."

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, who had planned to return home on Sunday after the latest three-week round of talks, said President Bill Clinton had asked him to remain in the region "because of the progress that was made today".
